name: ORBITER
summary: Thirty-seven metres of spaceplane: a 18.3 m payload bay with radiator-lined doors, a seven-seat crew module in the nose, a 15 m manipulator arm and three engines that each burned for eight and a half minutes at a time.

rooms.name: Flight Deck
rooms.description: Four seats under eleven windows, the largest flown on any spacecraft. Commander and pilot face a forward console; two mission specialists sit behind them, and the aft station looks back through overhead panes into the payload bay to fly the arm. Ascent is flown by computer, entry mostly so, and the last few hundred metres by hand at a 20° glide.

hotspots.title: Commander's Seat
hotspots.text: Left forward. Rotational hand controller on the right, speed brake on the left.

hotspots.title: Forward Console
hotspots.text: Glass cockpit after 1998; eleven CRTs before that.

hotspots.title: Aft Station
hotspots.text: Faces backwards into the bay, with its own hand controllers for the arm and for docking.

rooms.name: Mid Deck
rooms.description: Where the crew actually lived: three more seats for ascent, forty-two stowage lockers, a galley, a toilet and sleep stations clipped to the walls. Volume is 71 m³ across both decks. The side hatch is here, and so is the floor panel that opens into the equipment bay holding the air and water systems.

hotspots.title: Stowage Lockers
hotspots.text: Forty-two modular lockers; almost everything aboard lived in one.

hotspots.title: Galley
hotspots.text: Hot water, a convection oven and a food tray that strapped to a thigh.

rooms.name: Airlock
rooms.description: A 1.6 m cylinder with two hatches, on the mid deck or moved into the bay when a docking adapter was carried. Two astronauts pre-breathed and cycled through it for every spacewalk; the suits hung on its inner wall. Depressurisation took about half an hour, most of it purging nitrogen.

rooms.name: Payload Bay
rooms.description: Eighteen point three metres by four point six, sized for a satellite and its upper stage. The doors are structural once closed and carry the radiators that reject the orbiter's heat, which is why they opened within an hour of reaching orbit and stayed open until the deorbit burn. Thirteen bridge fittings along each sill take the payload loads.

hotspots.title: Radiator Panel
hotspots.text: Freon loops on the inside of each door; the bay opens on orbit or the orbiter overheats.

hotspots.title: Keel Fitting
hotspots.text: Takes the payload's side loads; the sill fittings take the rest.

rooms.name: Payload
rooms.description: A representative satellite on its cradle: 4.4 m long, 3.8 m across, with folded radiator panels and a berthing ring at the forward end. On a real flight this position carried anything from a communications satellite to a laboratory module, and the arm lifted it out through the open doors at a metre a minute.

rooms.name: Manipulator Arm
rooms.description: Fifteen point three metres of Canadian-built arm on the port sill, with six joints and an end effector that captures a grapple fixture by closing three wires around it. It cannot lift its own weight on the ground. On orbit it moved 30 t payloads, and later held astronauts on a foot restraint while they worked.

rooms.name: Orbital Manoeuvring System
rooms.description: Two pods either side of the tail, each with a 26.7 kN engine and the propellant for about 300 m/s of manoeuvring. They circularised the orbit after the tank was dropped, changed it during the flight, and fired retrograde to come home. The reaction control thrusters share their tanks and cluster around the same pods.

rooms.name: Main Engines
rooms.description: Three reusable engines burning hydrogen and oxygen from the external tank at 2,000 kg a second, throttled between 67 and 109 per cent for eight and a half minutes. Each cost about $40 million and was removed, inspected and reinstalled between flights. On orbit they are dead weight: everything after tank separation is done by the pods above them.

systems.name: Power
systems.description: Three fuel cells under the bay floor; the orbiter had no solar arrays and ran on cryogenic reactants.

systems.name: Atmos
systems.description: The crew module is the only pressurised volume; the bay is vacuum from doors-open to doors-closed.

systems.name: Thermal
systems.description: Freon loops from the crew module and avionics out to the radiators on the inside of the bay doors.

systems.name: Data
systems.description: Five general-purpose computers voting on every command, and the aft station's own arm controls.

segments.name: On Orbit
segments.caption: Thirty-seven metres, seven crew, and a cargo bay that took twenty-four tonnes to low orbit.

segments.name: Aft Fuselage
segments.caption: Three engines that burned for eight and a half minutes and were then dead weight for two weeks.

segments.name: Payload Bay
segments.caption: The doors are radiators. They opened within an hour of orbit and stayed open until the deorbit burn.

segments.name: Manipulator Arm
segments.caption: Fifteen metres of arm that could not lift itself on the ground and moved thirty tonnes in orbit.

segments.name: Flight Deck
segments.caption: Eleven windows, four seats, and a twenty-degree glide flown by hand at the end.

segments.name: Mid Deck
segments.caption: Where the crew actually lived: forty-two lockers, a galley and sleep stations on the wall.

segments.name: Airlock
segments.caption: Two at a time, forty minutes of pre-breathe, and out through the bay.

segments.name: Manoeuvring Pods
segments.caption: Three hundred metres a second of manoeuvring, and the burn that brought it home.
